message:
Help me complete and structure a type hierarchy. I'm formalizing "the organization of language" as one evolutionary tree rooted at the Word, generated by exactly three operators: aggregate (one -> many), refine (one -> same, with validation), specialize (one -> further specified). Full context and my current type sketch are attached.

Please give a structured, substantive answer to three questions:
(1) What types am I MISSING for completeness in the organization of language?
(2) Propose a precise type hierarchy that unifies the EVOLUTION ordering (how a thing grows: chapter -> book -> subject -> library) with the INHERITANCE ordering (is-a: Cover <: Chapter, Subject <: Book, Library <: Subject).
(3) Is "reference/pointer" a fourth operator beside the three, or is it derivable from refine?

Also weigh this analogy and tell me whether it dissolves the evolution-vs-inheritance tension: all living eukaryotes descend from a single-celled ancestor yet are multicellular, so the one-to-many (aggregate) step does NOT sever inheritance from the ancestor. Does aggregation itself act as a mode of inheritance -- the many descending from the one?

Aim for depth over breadth. I'll evaluate your answer against my own framework.
